name: Cayuse
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.source_named: Only vocabularies exist (Hale 1846; Henshaw; Aoki 1998 dictionary); Wikipedia article loaded contains no stress statement and names no grammar

sources.citation: Northwest Anthropology LLC. 2023. 50 Years of Northwest Anthropology: Archive of NARN/JONA Volumes 1-56, Memoirs 1-7 & 13 (Acrobat portfolio, 115 embedded PDFs). Free download from https://www.northwestanthropology.com/narnjona-digital-archive
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Container only; used to extract NARN 3(1) 1969 (attachment 52) and NARN 5(2) 1971 (attachment 96). Listed with pdfdetach -list; 1.5 GB.

Nothing on stress; states that 'Weyíiletpuu is a dialect of the Nez Perce language as used by the Cayuse people' and that 'a distinctive dialect of the Cayuse people has not been used since the 1940's and is designated as extinct' (identity warning: modern 'Cayuse' language teaching is Nez Perce, not cayu1241).

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: No phonology section and no stress statement; reproduces Hale's accented vocabulary and Rigsby 1969's pronoun/verb tables; bibliography = Aoki 1998, Hale 1846, Rigsby 1969 (with Google Books id _s2-DwAAQBAJ), Sapir 1929, UNESCO 2010. Used to find the JONA route to Rigsby 1969.

sources.citation: Sprague, Roderick (ed.), with linguistic notes by Haruo Aoki and Bruce Rigsby. 1971. Field notes and correspondence of the 1901 Field Columbian Museum expedition by Merton L. Miller to the Columbia Plateau. Northwest Anthropological Research Notes 5(2).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing; the 'linguistic notes' concern Sahaptin/Nez Perce object names in Miller's museum catalogue; the only Cayuse mention is a catalogue line ('From Cayuse.. Buckskin dress'). Not relevant.

sources.citation: Rigsby, Bruce. 1969. The Waiilatpuan Problem: More on Cayuse-Molala Relatability. Northwest Anthropological Research Notes 3(1): 68-146.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing on Cayuse stress placement. The fullest existing treatment of Cayuse (all sources: Townsend 1835, Hale 1841, McBean 1859, Henshaw 1888, Ray 1931-32, Jacobs 1930-31, Stern 1963, Rigsby 1964). p. 70: 'the impossibility of reconstituting the proper phonetic (and phonological) shapes of forms'; p. 143 n. 46: 'Cayuse phonetics, like those of other Pacific Northwest languages, appear to have been complex. I do not think that one can reasonably propose accurate reconstituted Cayuse forms in the absence of a single reliable and extensive corpus of phonetically-transcribed Cayuse forms'. Indiv…

sources.citation: Hale, Horatio. 1846. Ethnography and Philology (United States Exploring Expedition, vol. 6). Philadelphia: Lea & Blanchard. Waiilatpu family pp. 561-562; vocabulary pp. 570-629.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: No Cayuse stress statement. p. 561: 'We had no time to obtain any particular information respecting the structure of the Waiilatpu, but were assured that it differed radically from that of the Sahaptin.' The general orthography note in the Philology introduction says the acute accent marks 'the syllable on which the accent or emphasis should be laid'; Cayuse vocabulary items carry such marks (yúant 'man', pintét 'father', penín 'mother' per the Wikipedia reproduction; the archive.org scanned loses most of them) but no rule is given.
